answer: The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) is the core metric of economic evaluation. It is calculated as the difference in cost between two options divided by the difference in health effect, typically expressed as dollars per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). An ICER is judged against a willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold: a program is considered cost-effective when its cost per QALY falls below the threshold and not cost-effective when it exceeds it. Plotting incremental cost against incremental effect on the cost-effectiveness plane shows whether an option dominates or is dominated by its comparator.

faqs.q: How is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) calculated?
faqs.a: The ICER divides the difference in cost between two programs by the difference in health effect, usually yielding a dollar-per-QALY figure that summarizes the additional cost of each extra unit of health gained.

faqs.q: How do you decide whether an ICER is cost-effective?
faqs.a: Compare the ICER to a willingness-to-pay threshold. If the cost per QALY is below the threshold, such as $50,000, the program represents good value; if it is above, the program is not considered cost-effective.

faqs.q: What does the cost-effectiveness plane show?
faqs.a: The plane plots incremental cost on one axis and incremental effect on the other. The quadrant a program falls in reveals whether it is dominant, dominated, or a tradeoff requiring a threshold to judge.
